newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION - 1997 a good year for New Zealand assets.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - 1997 a good year for New Zealand assets.

text.p: By Stephen Toplis, economist at Doyle Paterson Brown Ltd

WELLINGTON, Aug 28 - 1997 should be a good year for investors in New Zealand assets. Perversely, this will be at a time when the economy produces one of its worst performances this decade. It is a simple story to tell.

In essence, slowing growth means falling inflationary pressure. This leads to an easing in monetary policy which drives bonds lower in yield and prepares the way for a resurgence in the equity market. There is nothing unusual in this. It is simply the standard investment cycle in progress.

Already economic growth has slowed. It will slow further. In the year to March 1996 GDP expanded 2.8 percent. This is significantly lower than the 5.2 percent in 1995 and 6.2 percent in 1994. Growth is likely to fall under 2.0 percent in the year to March 1997 before rebounding the year after on the back of tax cuts and the expected easing in monetary policy.
If there is a risk to this outlook it is that short term growth is actually weaker than anticipated as the dampening effect of ongoing tight monetary policy takes its toll.

As growth slows spare capacity in the economy develops. Already there is clear evidence this is occurring. In the June quarter of this year NZIER reported its capacity utilisation variable stood at 89.59 percent.

While this remains well above its long term average, implying that capacity is still tight, it is, nonetheless, falling. The latest reading is the lowest capacity utilisation has been since the third quarter of 1993 and well down from its peak of 91.13 percent in the fourth quarter of 1994.
Businesses are also reporting that the tightness in the labour market is easing. In the first quarter of this year a net majority of business reported it had become easier to find unskilled labour.

This was the first "easing" reported in over two years. A net 29 percent of businesses still reported that skilled labour was becoming more difficult to acquire but this was the lowest expression of difficulty recorded since December 1993.

These figures do not imply we are awash with spare capacity but they do show conditions are becoming easier. Moreover, with growth expected to fall from current levels, further alleviation of capacity constraints can be expected.

Another way of looking at this is to look at GDP relative to its trend. We assume trend GDP growth for New Zealand is 2.7 percent per annum or just under 0.7 percent per quarter. On this basis the economy has grown below trend in four of the last five quarters.

This is expected to remain the case for some time to come. This will ease pressure on the economy. The Reserve Bank seems to think trend growth of 3.0 percent is achievable. Therefore, the Bank must be becoming even more relaxed than we with the growth profile.

If growth slows and spare capacity begins to develop, inflationary pressures must wilt. Underlying inflation will thus be on its way down again by the end of the year. Annual underlying inflation is expected to peak at 2.6 percent in the year to September 1996 before falling to 1.6 percent by September 1997.

In all but the short term, the pressure on inflation must be down. However, our forecasts are for inflation to remain within the top quarter of the band for the foreseeable future. If this is the case then, unless the Bank relaxes the rigidity of its inflation target, real interest rates are condemned to stay high in this country for the foreseeable future.
Nonetheless with overall inflationary pressures abating, interest rates can only go one way.

On a twelve month basis we are confident that rates across the curve will be considerably lower than where they are now. This is particularly so at the short end. We believe the Bank will allow short rates to drift slowly lower over the remainder of this year before sanctioning a formal easing in the first quarter of next year.

We believe the Bank will be loathe to do anything before the election, given the potential downward pressures on the currency at the time, but may be convinced to move in the last quarter of this year if the evidence of a slowdown snowballs.

With short rates tumbling next year we believe the long bond must also track downward in yield. However, shorter term we are less optimistic that the rally will progress without a correction. We still expect to see a sell off in the United States before the end of this year and expect this to flow through domestically.

As interest rates fall the equity market's performance will be enhanced. This will be assisted by the outlook for continued positive economic growth and the transfer of domestic institutions' cash reserves into other securities as yields on short dated paper fall. As at the end of June domestic
institutions had 15 percent of their assets in domestic cash and it was rising.
In summary then:
- Growth and forecast growth is waning; - Annual inflation will soon begin to fall but forecast inflation will fall sooner;
- The Reserve Bank will formally ease monetary conditions before the end of the first quarter of 1997;
- This will result initially in a strong rally in bonds which will be followed up by a positive equity market performance.
(Note - The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters)
